\chapter{Heart}
\label{ch:mr-heart}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the heart in Marathi, name three English words that share its root, and say what makes it different from every other word this book has taken apart: it never drifted at all.}

The reader produces \mr{हृदय} and its three secure English cousins — heart, cordial, cardiac — then sets it against \mr{वाचणे}'s drift from speaking to reading, \mr{समजणे}'s drift from waking to understanding, and \mr{डोळा}'s replacement of the old eye-word, naming \mr{हृदय} as the one word among them that never drifted at all.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hṛdaya]{\mr{हृदय} (hṛdaya) — the word that never drifted}

\label{lesson:MR-C13-hrudaya}



\begin{quote}
The face is complete: \textbf{ḍoḷā, kān, tõḍ, nāk} — and \textbf{nāk} was the one whose English cousin, \textbf{nose}, needed no qualification at all. One organ is left, and its history could not be more different from \textbf{\mr{डोळा}}'s.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{हृदय}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{हृदय}} — \emph{hṛdaya} — \textbf{heart} (neuter)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
One new mark, thirteen chapters in: \textbf{\mr{ृ}}, the \textbf{vocalic \emph{r}} — a small hook below the consonant, standing for a syllabic \emph{r} sound with no vowel written beside it. \textbf{\mr{ह}}, \textbf{\mr{द}}, \textbf{\mr{य}} are all familiar. \emph{Hṛ-da-ya}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{हृदय}} continues Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{हृदय}} \emph{hṛdaya} itself, unchanged in shape since this book's earliest chapters were still explaining what a \emph{halant} does. Its root is Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*\'{k}ērd-}}, \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{} — and this is about as secure as a cognate gets: English \textbf{heart}, Latin \textbf{cor}/\textbf{cordis} (behind \textbf{cordial}), and Greek \textbf{kardia} (behind \textbf{cardiac}) are all the same word, diverging by ordinary sound change and nothing stranger.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Set \textbf{\mr{हृदय}} against the words this book has already taken apart. Chapter 11's \textbf{\mr{वाचणे}} drifted from \emph{vac-}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}to read\textquotedblright{} by way of a causative twist — reading as \emph{making the text speak}. The same chapter's \textbf{\mr{समजणे}} drifted from \emph{budh-}, \textquotedblleft{}to wake,\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}to understand\textquotedblright{} — an idea arriving is a kind of waking up. Chapter 15's \textbf{\mr{डोळा}} drifted furthest of all, from \emph{dola}, \textquotedblleft{}a swing,\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} pushing out the word it replaced. \textbf{\mr{हृदय}}, by contrast, has drifted almost nowhere: no causative twist, no metaphor, no replacement — the same word, doing the same job, since before Sanskrit was written down.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{hṛdaya} — heart
  \item \emph{Name:} three English words sharing its root — \textbf{heart, cordial, cardiac}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five body words this book has taught — \textbf{ḍoḷā, kān, tõḍ, nāk, hṛdaya}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name three English words that share \textbf{\mr{हृदय}}'s root. (\textbf{Heart}, \textbf{cordial}, \textbf{cardiac}.) What makes \textbf{\mr{हृदय}} different from \textbf{\mr{वाचणे}}, \textbf{\mr{समजणे}}, and \textbf{\mr{डोळा}}? (Those three \textbf{drifted} — speaking to reading, waking to understanding, swinging to eye; \textbf{\mr{हृदय}} did not drift at all.) What new Devanagari mark did this lesson add? (\textbf{\mr{ृ}}, the vocalic \emph{r}.)
